en: In the *Eyes of the Commentary on the Sūtra of Maitreya’s Descent*, it is said:
"If one rejoices only in the Pure Land, then sublime practice will not be perfected; if one hopes only for the celestial palaces, I fear that the superior causes will not be accomplished.
Although the Pure Land is free from defilement, the holy teachings themselves contain variations; although the celestial palaces possess sensual delights..."
The principle is certain and beyond doubt. For those who seek the objects of sensory desire, they are defiled by involvement with things yet remain undefiled;
for those who indulge in sensual pleasures, they are defiled by things that are not inherently defiling. Their precepts and karma are deficient, and their merit is meager.

Since the Buddha manifests in impure forms in response to the capacities of sentient beings, ordinary people likewise accord with the realm of the Sage and rejoice in such births. The highest sages and the most eminent worthies have all undertaken this practice.

Those of inferior rank and lower status—how could they possibly transcend this? Therefore, those whose conduct is identical should all lead with single-minded devotion; having already mastered the principles through diligent study, they may hope for the fulfillment of their causal conditions.
As for other details and traces of his life, they are fully recorded in separate biographies. The above account of the benefits bestowed upon the first heaven is hereby concluded.
Regarding the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born*, the preface states:
"In preparing to expound this sūtra, there are briefly three sections: first, the purpose of its composition; second, the explanation of its title; and third, the exposition of the text."
There are two reasons for his initial coming: first, it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings of inferior capacity.
Although Maitreya’s birth in heaven benefits those of superior and middling capacities, those of inferior capacity have not yet attained the benefit of entering the state of sainthood (*ārya*).

Second, it is to manifest the path of teaching in the human realm. Although the teachings in the heavens were previously and extensively revealed, the seven characteristics of the human realm [must now be shown].

Because he has not yet proclaimed [the teaching] for the purpose of transforming sentient beings, these two meanings lead to the discussion of the "subsequent birth" (下生) following the "birth above" (上生).
Second, regarding the explanation of the name, there are briefly three pairs: first, the pair of the speaker and the spoken; the Buddha’s preaching is the speaker.
...as well. "Maitreya and others" refers to that which is spoken. Second, the pair of the recipient and the received:

here, "Maitreya" is the name for the recipient, and "descending birth" (*adho-janman*) is the name for what is received. Third, the pair of the signified and the signifier: here, "Maitreya’s descending birth" is the name for the signified, and the "sūtra" is the name for the signifier.
Regarding the descending birth, there are three meanings: first, it is named as the initial entry into the womb; second, the entry [into the womb]...

The term "dwelling in birth" (*jāta*) is a general designation for the three [stages]. It is a collective expression for the human realm; although there are eight phases (*aṣṭa-nimitta*), the latter seven all occur within the human realm.
In contrast to the celestial realm, these are all considered "lower births. Thus, from the narrow to the broad, they are divided into three meanings, none of which contradict one another.
This refers to the fact that after the retribution of the celestial realm has ended, one is born again in the human realm; therefore, it is called a "lower birth."

It extensively discusses the deeds of the Holy One’s descent [to Jambudvīpa]; therefore, it is called the *Sūtra on the Descent* (*Xiasheng jing*). As for the title *Xiasheng jing*, it follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) analysis.
From "Thus have I heard" up to "five hundred people together," [the text continues].
The commentary states: In the second section of the third lecture, "Discerning the Benefits for the Transformation of Inferior Persons," there are two parts.

First, a brief discernment of the benefits for the transformation of sentient beings who are inferior persons; second, an extensive discernment of the benefits for the transformation of sentient beings who are inferior persons. Regarding these inferior persons:

There is naturally a distinction between superiority and inferiority; hence, there is this teaching of both concise and extensive versions. The former consists of three parts: first, the section on attesting faith and the transmission of the sutra;

second, the section on the extensive exposition through questions and answers; and third, the section on rejoicing in the teaching and putting it into practice. Such is the significance of these three parts.

This can be understood through reflection. This is the first [point]. There is an interpretation that this sutra also possesses a "preface of the occasion for the teaching" (*nidāna*), because from the words "At that time, Ānanda...
up to "he sat down," it initiates the discourse. This interpretation is incorrect.

For there is no other sutra where a question is posed and the Buddha provides an answer that is designated as a "preface" (*nidāna*) such that it could serve as a precedent. Why is this so? As [in the following example]:

To explain the teaching, it cannot be treated as a single uniform case. Sometimes, when each [Buddha] expounds the Dharma, they manifest light and cause the earth to tremble to summon the assembly as a condition, and only then preach the sutra;
or they may preach other sutras, in which case they simply proceed to speak without further manifest signs.

This sutra is like the latter case, and therefore lacks a prologue for the commencement of the teaching. Within this [prologue], there are five phrases; the middle three are the same as before. The first...
"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): this first indicates the Dharma that was heard; therefore, "thus" (*evam*) comes first, followed by "I have heard" (*mayā śrutam*).
Now, by employing the function of extensive learning and total retention (*bahuśruta-dhāraṇī*), one signifies the mastery of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; hence it is said, "Thus have I heard.
Alternatively, because the sequence differs between the languages of the Flower [India] and the Yi [China], either version may be retained as appropriate, and the meaning remains unimpaired. (500)

Regarding "people," as stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*: "World-Honored One, among these five hundred bhikṣus, how many bhikṣus have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*), how many have attained both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), and how many have attained wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukta*)? The World-Honored One replied:
"Śāriputra, among these five hundred bhikṣus, ninety bhikṣus have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge; [ninety...]"
A bhikṣu attains both-fold liberation (ubhayatobhāgavimukti), while other bhikṣus attain liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti).
By this it is known that the meaning of "triple-knowledge" (traividya) and "both-fold liberation" is also distinct.
Regarding the passage from "At that time Ānanda" up to "placed his right knee on the ground," the commentary states:
This constitutes the second question and answer. The detailed exposition consists of four parts: first, Ānanda’s request; second, the Tathāgata’s permission to speak; third...
"Because of past habitual tendencies," he said to the World-Honored One, "[until] all are fully understood. The commentary states:
The second [section], the praise of the noble ones, has two parts: first, a general praise; second, a specific praise. This is the former. As for the matter:

This refers to the method of summary; thus, it is a general statement. Because one wishes to request [the teaching on] Maitreya’s future activity of transformation and guidance, it is necessary to praise the three types of penetrating wisdom (*trividya*).
The passage from "All past Buddhas" up to "all know this" [expresses this].
The commentary states: The second section, the specific praise, has three parts. First, the praise of past wisdom; next, the praise of present wisdom;
and finally, the praise of future wisdom. The first part [of the past wisdom] also has three sub-sections: first, the capacity for transformation; second, the time of transformation;
and third, the assembly transformed. This is the first [sub-section]. "Lineage" (gotra) refers to one's clan. Vipaśyin Buddha was born of the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Kauṇḍinya. Śikhin...
The lineage of Buddha Viśvabhū was likewise. Buddha Krakucchanda was born into the Brahmin caste and had the clan name Kāśyapa.
Buddha Kanakamuni and Buddha Kāśyapa were also the same. "Word" (*nāman*) refers to the name given at twenty years of age;

"name" (*nāma*) refers to the name given at birth. "Title" (*abhidhāna*) refers to the Ten Epithets. "Disciples" refers to the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, which is easily understood. "Voice" (*ghoṣa*)... [text fragment].
It is heard that the Bodhisattvas assist the World-Honored One; thus they are called "winged attendants" (*yi cong*). "Winged" (*yi*) means to assist or to accomplish.
The Buddha Vipaśyin preached the Dharma in three assemblies: the first consisted of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand people, the second ten thousand, and the last eight thousand.
The Buddha Śikhin also preached in three assemblies: the first consisted of one hundred thousand, the second eighty thousand, and the last seventy thousand.
Vipaśyin Buddha held two assemblies to preach the Dharma: the first consisted of seventy thousand people, and the second of sixty thousand.
Krakucchanda Buddha held one assembly to preach the Dharma, consisting of forty thousand people. Kanakamuni Buddha held one assembly to preach the Dharma.
There were thirty thousand people. At one assembly where Kāśyapa Tathāgata preached the Dharma, there were twenty thousand people.
Śākyamuni showed [this] at one assembly, where there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people. When the sutra speaks of "more or less," its meaning lies herein.
This is explained in detail in the first fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
"Observing all throughout one kalpa and a hundred kalpas" is described as the second [knowledge]:
knowing the time for transformation. As it says in the *Sūtra on Requesting the Buddha* regarding the absence of a close relative:
"The first Buddha was named Vipaśyin; since his parinirvāṇa ninety-one kalpas ago, the second Buddha was named Śikhin."
Since the Parinirvāṇa of the first Buddha, thirty-one kalpas have passed. The third Buddha was named Sūryaprabha;
since his Parinirvāṇa, it has likewise been thirty-one kalpas. Within this Bhadrakalpa, there shall be five hundred Buddhas.
The first was Krakucchanda Buddha; ten thousand years have passed since his parinirvāṇa. The second was Kanakamuni Buddha;
ten thousand years have passed since his parinirvāṇa. The third was Kāśyapa Buddha; ten thousand years have passed since his parinirvāṇa.
The fourth Buddha is myself, Śākyamuni Buddha. Some say that since he is called Vi... [text continues]

Since the parinirvāṇas of the three Buddhas beginning with Vipaśyin have occurred ninety-one and thirty-one kalpas ago respectively, one might conclude that the parinirvāṇas of the remaining three Buddhas have likewise occurred ten thousand years ago; this is an error. It is not so. Why?
Thus, when compared to the time of the parinirvāṇa of the three previous Buddhas during this Bhadrakalpa of Śākyamuni,
it is said to be ninety-one kalpas and thirty-one kalpas [respectively]. Although Krakucchanda Buddha appeared when the human lifespan was forty thousand years,

Kanakamuni Buddha appeared when it was thirty thousand years, and Kāśyapa Buddha appeared when it was twenty thousand years, these immediately preceding Buddhas, when compared to [the present one], are...

Regarding the previous Buddhas, they are thus called "Ten Thousand Years" (Wansui), yet this was not during the time of Śākyamuni; compared to the three preceding Buddhas, all were "Ten Thousand Years.
The names, surnames, and parents of the seven Buddhas, as well as their first disciples under the Bodhi tree and their pairs of attendants and disciples, are detailed at length in those [scriptures].
"Furthermore, [he knows] the names and surnames of the people.

The commentary states: "This refers to the subsequent transformation of the assembly. According to the *Wuyan jing* (Sūtra of No-Extension), the father of Vipaśyin Buddha was named Bāntan, a Kṣatriya king;
his mother was named Pātumati; the kingdom he governed was named Pātumati. The father of Śikhin Buddha was named Ā..."
The Cakravartin Kṣatriya King’s mother was named Parāvatī; the kingdom he ruled was called Aruṇama.
The father of the Buddha Anūpa was the Kṣatriya King Jyotipāla; his mother was named Jayasikhi; the kingdom he ruled was called Arumukha.
The father of the Buddha Krakucchanda was of the Brāhmaṇa caste, named Ajita; his mother was named Cunna.
O Ajita, the capital city governed by him has three aspects:
first, its substance; second, its dimensions; and third, its adornment. This refers to the first. Although it does not yet exist at present, it shall exist in the future;
therefore, it is said that it "shall exist" within the center. The royal city is surrounded on all sides by guards of the city walls.

The place where the people reside is named Kuò. The *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* states: "Translated as Tóu-mì; formerly called Yǒu-chuāng (Possessing a Banner), now [called] Huì-chuāng (Wisdom Banner).
Although the terminology differs, the meaning is not contradictory. Why is this? The fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"At that time, the Holy King erected a great precious banner, sixteen *xún* in circumference and one thousand *xún* in height, adorned with various colors."
The banner has one hundred *gu* [sections]; each *gu* has one hundred branches. It is woven from precious threads and interspersed with various jewels.
When the Holy King carries this banner, he bestows it upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor within the kingdom.

Because it is known that this banner exists within the city, it is called "Possessing the Banner" (*yǒuchí*). Furthermore, because he bestows this banner upon śramaṇas and others, it is called "Wisdom" (*huì*).
Although the term *dhvaja* (banner/pole) has two meanings, because the city resembles a cock's head (*kīṭa*), it is collectively named "Cock's Head" (*Kīṭa*).
Some say that in Sanskrit it is called *Kīṭamukha*, which is the opposite of "Cock's Head. This interpretation is incorrect; for the *Buddhabhāṣita-sūtra* states:
"There is a land with a city named Kīṭamukha."
Regarding the phrase "twelve (up to) seven *yojanas* from east to west," the *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"This refers to the dimensions of the city. Taicheng (Great Buddha) says: "It is one thousand two hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, and seven *yojanas* in height.
As for the discrepancy between this [text] stating twelve *yojanas* and that [source], it is because their periods of prosperity and decline differ; this will be explained below.

This should be understood as follows: it represents the instruction of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) to follow the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*), because he practices them simultaneously on his own level;

thus, twelve *yojanas*. Because a Dharma-King necessarily possesses the seven jewels (*saptaratna*), [it is] seven *yojanas*. Furthermore, although one receives superior retribution, one does not transcend the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*);
thus, twelve *yojanas*. Because one is not separated from the seven realms of existence (*bhava*) and the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), [it is] seven.
Yojanas. Regarding the phrase "the land is rich and fertile" up to "the royal streets are fit for practitioners," the commentary states:
Following this is the description of the city’s adornments. Although there are many such adornments, they are briefly summarized into three types: the land, the people, and [the royal streets].
The streets and alleys are as extensively explained below.
At that time, from within the city... [until] "...those who requested peace," the commentary states:
"The second dragon king added his excellence. The *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* says: "There was a great powerful dragon king named..."

*Tāraśikhi* is now called "Water Light" (*Jishui guang*); these are alternate designations based on the respective traditions of the Flower [continent] and the Barbarians, and thus they do not contradict one another.
At that time, from within the city of Kukkutapada (the Rooster Peak), up to the point where it was said to be "extremely fragrant and pure."
The commentary states: Third is the removal of evil by spirits and deities. The *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* says:
"There is a great yakṣa deity named Bhadrapāla-saṃgha; in the Qin language, this means 'Good and Auspicious' (Shànhǎo), while the current name is Yèhuā, which belongs to the same category as Shànhǎo.
In Sanskrit, it is called *yakṣa*, which here means 'violent and wicked,' or alternatively 'valiant. This is the name of the deity, who possesses supernatural powers.
Regarding "ghosts and animals": what is here called a *rākṣasa* is precisely that which is to be feared.
Since both yakṣas and rākṣasas exist in that city, it is not contradictory to mention either one interchangeably. "Dharma" refers to principle; "teaching" refers to verbal instruction.
Practice follows principle because it does not transgress the sacred word.
"Ānanda, you should know... up to one hundred thousand *yojanas*. The commentary states:
Regarding the second land, its vastness and excellence are twofold. First, the increase and decrease of the water on the initial land; second, the ancillary explanation resolving doubts.

The first [section] further has three parts: first, the increase of the land; next, the simultaneous decrease of both land and water; and finally, distinguishing the decrease of the water alone. This is the first [part].
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Attainment of Buddhahood* states: "At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was ten thousand yojanas long and eight thousand yojanas wide;
the waters of the four great oceans gradually receded by three thousand yojanas.
The sixth fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The land of Jambudvīpa was seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; the waters receded by three [thousand yojanas]."

The ground [of the world] is originally seven thousand *yojanas* thick; thus, it is ten thousand *yojanas* in total. Now, this sutra states that it is one hundred thousand *yojanas*, which is difficult to reconcile.
One interpretation holds that this difference exists because [the teaching] accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
This explanation is not correct, for there should be no contradiction with the text when providing a reconciliation. I now offer this explanation: at the time when Maitreya first appears, the four...

Because the ocean waters decrease significantly while the land increases greatly, after a long period of time, the ocean waters gradually increase again until they reach one hundred thousand *yojanas*, as the land consequently becomes narrow and diminished.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which explains this in detail, it is six thousand five hundred *yojanas*;
however, there are further discrepancies in the texts, which may be reconciled by applying this same principle.
"Regarding 'all mountains, rivers, and rocks... shall all be completely extinguished,' the commentary states:
'Next... [omitted] ...like a mirror that is clear and bright.'"
The commentary states: The second section provides an auxiliary explanation to resolve doubts. There are six such doubts: first, the doubt that although it is vast, it may not be level;

second, the doubt that although it is level, there may be no grain; third, the doubt that although there is grain, there may be no people; fourth, the doubt that although there are people, they may lack treasures;

fifth, the doubt that although there are treasures, there may be no villages; sixth, the doubt that although there are villages, there may be no trees or fruit. Since there are six doubts, there are likewise six resolutions.
1. The decision that it is vast and necessarily level and even; 2. The decision that the five grains are abundant and level; 3. The decision that grain and food suffice for the people;
4. The decision that the people possess rare treasures; 5. The decision that treasures flourish in the villages; 6. The decision that the hamlets have sweet fruits. Regarding this first doubt:
although the earth may be one hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent, it is not necessarily level and even; therefore, it is said that "the ground is level and even. As [it says]:
The mirror is clear and bright. In reality, there were also various mountains at that time; however, because they are being contrasted with the present time, it is said they were "level and even.
Otherwise, this would contradict the following passage, which states that Mahākāśyapa dwells on this mountain. Question:

Before the kalpa of destruction has occurred and Maitreya has already appeared, by what cause and condition are there no mountains? Answer: It is based on [the fact that] after his parinirvāṇa, all the bhikṣus...
“Kauṇḍinya, after my parinirvāṇa, one hundred years hence, listen, my disciples, the śramaṇas:
there will be those who are clever and wise, no different from me. After a thousand years, during the three hundred-year period [thereafter], there will be great chaos and calamity.”

The myriad afflictions and transformations will press upon one's person, and billions of calamities will arise. The population will be nearly extinguished, for at that time there shall be a great flood twenty *li* high.
It shall purify all famous mountains, remaining for twelve full years before it finally recedes; thereafter, no mountains shall remain in their former locations.
The land was governed with perfect justice, and its happiness was beyond description.

The youth Candraprabha then appeared in the world and, through the Prajñāpāramitā, taught the people so that those who attained the Way numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands daily; those reborn in the heavens were beyond counting.
At that time, the people stood eight feet tall and lived for one hundred and eighty thousand years. There were times when the population increased greatly.
They ate what was provided naturally. The people thought only of the Way and made no use of gold or jewels. Sages filled the land.
The palaces, temples, and city walls were all made of the seven treasures. The Dharma King ruled the world for fifty-two years and then departed.
From that time on, the Dharma gradually declined. Then, Mālunkyāputra, he took the Buddha’s *śarīra* from the various stūpas and temples and gathered them together in one place.
Only after dwelling there will he enter parinirvāṇa. The Dragon King should then take the relics and the Buddha’s twelvefold canon and offer them within the ocean.
Thereafter, the Great Dharma will come to an end. The people of later times will have a lifespan of forty or fifty years before they pass away;
at that time, when the human lifespan is five years, there will be no kings, ministers, or officials.
At that time, five years of age will be equivalent to one year of our present era. When human life is about to end, the great ocean will shrink and all its waters will boil and surge violently.
The continent of Jambudvīpa will become vast, level, and even; it is then that Maitreya Buddha shall bring it to completion.
Regarding the passage from "In Jambudvīpa" to "grain is abundant and cheap," the commentary states:
The second doubt is that although the land may be level and even, it is not necessarily the case that the five grains will flourish; therefore, this explanation is provided.
Regarding the phrase "the population is flourishing," the commentary states:
The third doubt is that although grain may be produced, it does not necessarily follow that there are people to possess the grain; therefore, these words were spoken.
Regarding the phrase "abounding in many rare treasures," the commentary states:
This addresses the fourth doubt, which says that although the population may flourish and grain may be abundant, it is not necessarily the case that there are various rare treasures;
therefore, this explanation is provided.
Regarding the phrase "the crowing of roosters reaching one another," the commentary states:
The fifth doubt says that although there may be many treasures, it is not necessarily the case that villages are situated close to one another; therefore, this interpretation was made.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, inferior flowers... to "...all grow in other places," the commentary states:
The sixth doubt asks, "Even though villages may be adjacent, it is not necessarily the case that there are trees with sweet fruit.
Therefore, this explanation was provided.
Commentary on the Sūtra Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, Scroll II.
